goldens.comment: The parseRefreshTokenResponse function incorrectly sets refresh_token to the hardcoded string 'refresh_token' when it's missing from the OAuth refresh token response. This invalidates the token, breaking subsequent token refreshes and causing authentication failures.

The Zod schema in parseRefreshTokenResponse uses computed property keys [z.string().toString()] and [z.string().optional().toString()] in minimumTokenResponseSchema, which is invalid Zod syntax and will throw a runtime error.

parseRefreshTokenResponse returns a Zod safeParse result ({ success, data, error }), not the credential key object. Persisting that as key stores the wrapper instead of the token payload; we should store the parsed data or use schema parse.

When APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT are set, the refreshFunction helper returns the fetch Response, but several callers (for example GoogleCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting res.data, and HubspotCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting a HubspotToken) assume it returns the integration-specific token object. That mismatch will cause runtime errors in the sync-enabled path unless the return type or those call sites are adjusted.

When the sync endpoint path is used, res is a fetch Response and has no .data; res?.data will be undefined and token.access_token will throw at runtime. This relies on a consistent return shape from refreshOAuthTokens, which isn’t guaranteed currently.

The `refreshOAuthTokens` function is passed `credentialId` instead of `userId`, which breaks the credential sync functionality by causing incorrect user lookups. This issue can lead to failures in syncing user credentials, impacting user experience.

The Salesforce integration checks `response.statusText` instead of `response.ok` when handling OAuth token refresh responses. This can lead to unreliable behavior, as a successful response may not be correctly identified, resulting in the use of stale credentials and potential authentication failures.

The `jsforce.Connection` is created using stale `credentialKey.access_token` and `credentialKey.instance_url` after a token refresh, which can lead to authentication failures and incorrect data access. Ensure that the connection is established using the refreshed token values instead.

The `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse` function can throw on invalid payloads, resulting in 500 Internal Server Errors instead of the expected 400 Bad Request responses. This can lead to confusion for clients and hinder proper error handling.

adjudication_records.issue_text: apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts:22-27 — webhook secret compared with `!==` on the raw header: not constant-time, and the header may be `string[]`; should use `crypto.timingSafeEqual` on normalized, length-checked buffers

adjudication.rationale: In `apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts` the code directly compares `req.headers[headerName] !== process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET`. In Next.js/Node, `req.headers[...]` is typed/behaves as `string | string[] | undefined`; if the header is provided multiple times it can be a `string[]`, and the direct `!==` comparison against a string will always fail, incorrectly rejecting valid requests. Also, using a normal string comparison for a shared secret is not constant-time; a timing-safe comparison on normalized buffers (with length check) is the standard mitigation for timing attacks when validating secrets.

adjudication_records.issue_text: apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts:22 — Node lowercases header keys but `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME` is free-form, so any uppercase in the env value makes the lookup undefined and rejects all requests

adjudication.rationale: In `apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts`, the secret is read via `req.headers[process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME || "calcom-webhook-secret"]`. In Node/Next, `req.headers` keys are normalized to lowercase, so indexing with a header name containing any uppercase letters (e.g. `"Calcom-Webhook-Secret"`) will not match the stored lowercase key and will yield `undefined`, causing the comparison to fail and all requests to be rejected. The diff adds only a comment saying it “should be in lowercase” but does not enforce lowercasing in code.

adjudication_records.issue_text: apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts:17 — no HTTP method check, so GET/DELETE/etc. reach the handler; should be restricted to POST

adjudication.rationale: The new Next.js API route `apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts` exports a handler that never checks `req.method`. As written, any HTTP method (GET/DELETE/etc.) will execute the same logic and then attempt `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body)`, which will throw for methods that typically have no body (e.g., GET), likely resulting in an unhandled error/500 instead of a proper 405/POST-only contract. Restricting to POST (and returning 405 otherwise) is a concrete missing check in the diff.

refreshOAuthTokens.ts:8-15 — the outbound request to `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` has no authentication/signature and the response status is never checked, so non-2xx or HTML error pages are passed downstream as token payloads

adjudication.rationale: In `packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/refreshOAuthTokens.ts`, when `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED && process.env.CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT && userId` is true, it does a plain `fetch(process.env.CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT, { method: "POST", body: new URLSearchParams(...) })` with no auth/signature headers or secret included, and it returns the `Response` without checking `response.ok`/status or validating content-type/body. That means non-2xx responses (including HTML error pages) can be returned to callers; at least some call sites (e.g., GoogleCalendarService expecting `res.data`) do not perform an explicit status check before using the result, so the core issue in the finding is present in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts:60-89 — decrypted `keys` blob is written to `credential.key` with no validation against the app's key schema

adjudication.rationale: In apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts the handler decrypts reqBody.keys and immediately does `const keys = JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...))`, then persists it to Prisma via `data: { key: keys }` on both update and create paths. The only checks performed are that the user exists, the app slug exists in DB, and that app metadata exists; there is no validation of the decrypted `keys` structure against any per-app credential/key schema (e.g., the zod schemas used elsewhere like googleCredentialSchema). This means malformed or unexpected key shapes can be stored and later break integrations, and the finding is directly supported by the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts:60-89 — the find-then-create is not atomic, so concurrent webhooks for the same user+app both miss `findFirst` and create duplicate credential rows; needs an upsert or transaction

adjudication.rationale: The new webhook handler does a read-then-write sequence: `credential.findFirst({ where: { userId, appId }})` and, if none, `credential.create(...)`. This is not done in a transaction and is not an atomic upsert. With concurrent webhook deliveries for the same `userId` + `appSlug`, both requests can observe “no row” and both attempt `create`, which can lead to duplicate credential rows (if no DB uniqueness constraint exists) or an unhandled unique-constraint error (if one does). The non-atomic pattern is directly visible in lines ~60-89 of the added file.

adjudication_records.issue_text: apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts — new credential-writing endpoint ships with no tests for the secret check, disabled-feature path, decryption failure, or create-vs-update behavior

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a new API route `apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts` but does not include any accompanying test changes. However, the proposed finding asserts there are *no tests* for specific behaviors (secret check, disabled feature, decryption failure, create-vs-update). From the diff alone, we can only verify that no new tests were added here—not that the codebase lacks existing coverage (e.g., shared API-route tests) for those paths. Also, “missing tests” is not, by itself, a concrete bug/security/correctness defect shown in the code changes.

adjudication_records.issue_text: .env.example:240-242 — comment says the key "must be 32 bytes for AES256" but suggests `openssl rand -base64 24` (24 bytes → 32-character string), so self-hosters generate a key the decrypt call rejects

adjudication.rationale: In .env.example the new comments state the encryption key "must be 32 bytes for AES256" but then suggest generating it with `openssl rand -base64 24`, which produces 24 random bytes (encoded to a ~32-character base64 string). That is an internal inconsistency in the diff and can mislead self-hosters about the required key material/length. However, the claim that the decrypt call will definitely reject such a key is not verifiable from the diff because `symmetricDecrypt`’s key expectations aren’t shown.
